set: Pharmacology: Drug Absorption, Metabolism and Adverse Reactions

questions.stem: A patient receives a medication by intravenous injection. What is the absolute bioavailability of the administered drug?
options: Approximately 50%
Exactly 100%
Approximately 75%
Dependent on gastric emptying
questions.explanation: Intravenous administration delivers the entire administered dose directly into the systemic circulation, giving an absolute bioavailability of 100%. Other routes may have lower bioavailability because of incomplete absorption or presystemic elimination.
questions.source: General Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetics - Bioavailability

questions.stem: A drug undergoes glucuronidation in the liver, producing a more water-soluble metabolite that can be eliminated in urine. Which category of metabolic reaction does glucuronidation represent?
options: Phase I oxidation
Phase I hydrolysis
Phase I reduction
Phase II conjugation
questions.explanation: Glucuronidation is a Phase II conjugation reaction in which glucuronic acid is attached to a drug or its metabolite. This generally increases water solubility and facilitates elimination through urine or bile.
questions.source: General Pharmacology: Drug Biotransformation - Phase II Reactions

questions.stem: A patient taking an antihypertensive drug develops excessive hypotension after the prescribed dose is increased. The reaction is predictable from the drug's known pharmacological action. How should this adverse drug reaction be classified?
options: Type A (augmented) reaction
Type B (bizarre) reaction
Type C (chronic) reaction
Type D (delayed) reaction
questions.explanation: Type A adverse drug reactions are predictable consequences of a drug's pharmacological effects and are commonly dose-related. Excessive blood-pressure reduction following an increased antihypertensive dose is a typical example.
questions.source: Adverse Drug Reactions: Type A and Type B Classification

questions.stem: A drug is completely absorbed from the intestine but undergoes extensive metabolism in the intestinal wall and liver before reaching the systemic circulation. What is the principal consequence of this presystemic metabolism?
options: Increased renal clearance of unchanged drug
Increased binding of drug to plasma proteins
Reduced systemic bioavailability of the parent drug
Reduced absorption across the intestinal epithelium
questions.explanation: First-pass metabolism removes part of the absorbed parent drug before it reaches systemic circulation. This lowers the oral bioavailability of the unchanged drug even when intestinal absorption is complete.
questions.source: General Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetics - First-Pass Effect

questions.stem: A patient receiving a stable dose of an active drug metabolized by CYP3A4 begins taking a strong CYP3A4 inducer. The drug has no active metabolites, and its clearance depends mainly on this enzyme. What change is most likely after enzyme induction is established?
options: Increased elimination half-life of the active drug
Decreased plasma exposure to the active drug
Increased plasma exposure to the active drug
Decreased hepatic metabolism of the active drug
questions.explanation: Enzyme induction increases the capacity of the relevant metabolic pathway and generally increases clearance of an active substrate. Consequently, plasma exposure may fall, potentially reducing therapeutic efficacy.
questions.source: Drug Metabolism: Enzyme Induction and Drug Interactions

questions.stem: A patient previously sensitized to penicillin develops sudden urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension within minutes of receiving penicillin again. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?
options: Predictable toxicity caused by cumulative drug exposure
Direct tissue injury caused by excessive drug concentration
Progressive toxicity caused by impaired renal elimination
Immediate hypersensitivity mediated by drug-specific IgE
questions.explanation: IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity can cause rapid mast-cell activation following re-exposure to an allergen. The resulting mediator release can produce urticaria, bronchospasm and potentially life-threatening anaphylaxis.
questions.source: Adverse Drug Reactions: Immunologically Mediated Drug Hypersensitivity

questions.stem: An uncharged, lipid-soluble drug crosses intestinal epithelial membranes mainly by passive diffusion. Assuming membrane properties, surface area and all other conditions remain constant, which TWO changes would directly increase its rate of passive diffusion? Choose TWO.
options: An increased concentration gradient across the membrane
An increased thickness of the epithelial membrane
An increased lipid permeability of the membrane to the drug
A decreased effective surface area available for diffusion
An increased molecular diffusion distance through the membrane
questions.explanation: Fick's law indicates that passive diffusion increases with a larger concentration gradient and greater membrane permeability. Greater diffusion distance or reduced surface area decreases the diffusion rate. These relationships help explain how physicochemical properties affect membrane transport.
questions.source: General Pharmacology: Drug Absorption - Passive Diffusion and Fick's Law

questions.stem: A patient takes a drug that is primarily cleared by CYP2D6-mediated metabolism. A potent CYP2D6 inhibitor is added, and the parent drug itself produces the therapeutic effect. Assuming no compensatory clearance pathway, what is the expected result?
options: Increased exposure to the active parent drug
Decreased exposure to the active parent drug
Increased conversion to inactive metabolites
Decreased elimination half-life of the parent drug
questions.explanation: Inhibition of a major drug-metabolizing enzyme reduces metabolic clearance of its substrate. For an active parent drug, this commonly raises systemic exposure and may increase the risk of concentration-dependent toxicity.
questions.source: Drug Metabolism: Enzyme Inhibition and Drug Interactions

questions.stem: A patient repeatedly develops a sharply demarcated, round, reddish-purple skin patch at exactly the same location after taking a particular medication. The lesion resolves with residual hyperpigmentation after the medication is stopped. Which adverse drug reaction is most likely?
options: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Fixed drug eruption
Drug-induced urticaria
questions.explanation: Fixed drug eruption characteristically recurs at the same anatomical site following re-exposure to the causative medication. The lesions are often well defined and commonly leave post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation after resolution.
questions.source: Adverse Drug Reactions: Drug-Induced Skin Eruptions

questions.stem: For most orally administered drugs absorbed through the gastrointestinal epithelium, which anatomical region provides the largest effective surface area for absorption?
options: Esophagus
Stomach
Large intestine
Small intestine
questions.explanation: The small intestine is the principal absorption site for most orally administered drugs because its folds, villi and microvilli create an extensive absorptive surface. Its blood supply and epithelial characteristics also favor drug uptake.
questions.source: General Pharmacology: Drug Absorption - Gastrointestinal Absorption

questions.stem: An orally administered prodrug has negligible intrinsic activity and must be converted by CYP2C19 into its active metabolite. A potent CYP2C19 inhibitor is introduced. Assume this is the dominant activation pathway and that no alternative pathway compensates. Which TWO changes are expected? Choose TWO.
options: Increased formation of the active metabolite
Decreased exposure to the active metabolite
Increased metabolic conversion of the prodrug
Increased exposure to the unchanged prodrug
Increased clearance of the unchanged prodrug
questions.explanation: Inhibiting the enzyme responsible for prodrug activation reduces formation of the active metabolite and may reduce therapeutic efficacy. Because less prodrug is converted, exposure to the unchanged parent compound can increase when that pathway dominates its clearance.
questions.source: Drug Metabolism: Prodrugs and Pharmacogenetic Drug Interactions

questions.stem: A patient develops a widespread painful rash, oral mucosal erosions, fever and epidermal detachment several days after starting a new medication. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is suspected. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Continue treatment while adding an oral antihistamine
Stop the suspected drug and arrange emergency hospital assessment
Reduce the medication dose and monitor the rash at home
Continue the medication and apply a topical corticosteroid
questions.explanation: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a potentially life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse reaction involving skin and mucous membranes. The suspected causative drug must be stopped immediately, and urgent hospital assessment and supportive management are required.
questions.source: Adverse Drug Reactions: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

questions.stem: A patient taking oral tetracycline begins taking a calcium supplement at the same time as each antibiotic dose. What is the most likely effect on tetracycline absorption?
options: Reduced absorption due to formation of poorly absorbed complexes
Increased absorption due to enhanced intestinal transport
Unchanged absorption because calcium acts only in the colon
Increased absorption due to reduced hepatic first-pass metabolism
questions.explanation: Calcium ions can form poorly absorbed chelate complexes with tetracyclines in the gastrointestinal tract. This reduces the amount of antibiotic available for absorption and can compromise treatment effectiveness.
questions.source: Drug Absorption: Chelation and Interactions with Divalent Cations

questions.stem: A drug undergoes oxidation by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes. Which category of drug metabolism includes this reaction?
options: Phase II acetylation
Phase II glucuronidation
Phase I functionalization
Phase II sulfation
questions.explanation: Oxidation is a Phase I functionalization reaction that chemically modifies a drug molecule, often by introducing or exposing a functional group. These reactions may alter pharmacological activity or prepare a compound for subsequent conjugation.
questions.source: General Pharmacology: Drug Biotransformation - Phase I Reactions

questions.stem: A patient with documented penicillin-specific IgE experiences an immediate allergic response after accidental re-exposure. Which TWO clinical findings are characteristic of IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity? Choose TWO.
options: Rapid-onset urticaria
Progressive liver fibrosis developing over several years
Acute bronchospasm
Cumulative peripheral neuropathy after months of treatment
Delayed bone marrow suppression caused by cytotoxicity
questions.explanation: Immediate IgE-mediated hypersensitivity triggers mast-cell degranulation, producing manifestations such as urticaria, angioedema and bronchospasm. These symptoms can develop within minutes and may progress to systemic anaphylaxis. Chronic fibrosis and cumulative toxicities are not characteristic immediate IgE-mediated effects.
questions.source: Adverse Drug Reactions: Type I Immediate Hypersensitivity

questions.stem: Two oral formulations contain the same dose of a drug. One is immediate-release and the other is extended-release. Both have equal total bioavailability, but the extended-release product releases the drug more gradually. Which concentration-time profile is generally expected for the extended-release formulation?
options: An earlier Tmax with a higher Cmax
A later Tmax with a lower Cmax
An earlier Tmax with a lower Cmax
A later Tmax with a higher Cmax
questions.explanation: Extended-release formulations generally slow the rate at which drug enters systemic circulation, producing a later time to peak concentration (Tmax) and a lower peak concentration (Cmax). When total bioavailability is equal, the overall exposure measured by AUC can remain similar despite differences in peak and timing.
questions.source: Biopharmaceutics: Immediate-Release and Extended-Release Dosage Forms

questions.stem: In an adult with normal physiology, which organ is the principal site of metabolism for most drugs that undergo extensive enzymatic biotransformation?
options: Spleen
Pancreas
Thyroid gland
Liver
questions.explanation: The liver is the major site of drug biotransformation because hepatocytes contain numerous metabolizing enzymes, including cytochrome P450 systems and conjugation enzymes. Drug metabolism can also occur in extrahepatic tissues, including the intestine and kidneys.
questions.source: General Pharmacology: Drug Metabolism - Hepatic and Extrahepatic Metabolism

questions.stem: A national pharmacovigilance system receives spontaneous reports of suspected adverse reactions to a newly marketed drug. Why can these reports alone not establish the true population incidence of the reaction?
options: The total exposed population and completeness of reporting are unknown
The reports contain only reactions confirmed by controlled clinical trials
The system records only reactions associated with excessive doses
The reports exclude reactions occurring after drug discontinuation
questions.explanation: Spontaneous reporting systems are valuable for detecting potential safety signals but are affected by underreporting, selective reporting and uncertain exposure denominators. Without reliable numbers of exposed patients and all occurring events, the true incidence cannot be calculated from reports alone.
questions.source: Pharmacovigilance: Spontaneous Reporting Systems and Their Limitations

questions.stem: A patient develops acute liver injury after a large acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose. Excess production of the reactive metabolite NAPQI is involved. Which TWO biochemical changes are central to the development of hepatotoxicity? Choose TWO.
options: Increased detoxification of NAPQI by unlimited glucuronidation
Depletion of hepatic glutathione needed to neutralize NAPQI
Accumulation of NAPQI that reacts with cellular proteins
Complete inhibition of acetaminophen absorption in the intestine
Conversion of NAPQI into a harmless metabolite without a cofactor
questions.explanation: During acetaminophen overdose, normal conjugation pathways become insufficient to handle the full dose, and increased amounts of the toxic metabolite NAPQI are formed. Hepatic glutathione stores become depleted, allowing NAPQI to bind cellular proteins and cause hepatocellular injury. N-acetylcysteine helps restore glutathione-dependent detoxification.
questions.source: Drug Metabolism and Toxicology: Acetaminophen Biotransformation and Overdose

questions.stem: A weakly acidic drug has a pKa of 4.0. The drug is present in gastric fluid at pH 2.0 and intestinal fluid at pH 6.0. Assuming acid-base equilibrium, which statement correctly describes the relative ionization of the drug?
options: It is predominantly ionized at pH 2.0 and unionized at pH 6.0
It is approximately equally ionized at both pH values
It is predominantly unionized at pH 2.0 and ionized at pH 6.0
It remains predominantly unionized at both pH values
questions.explanation: Weak acids are predominantly protonated and unionized when environmental pH is below their pKa. When pH rises above their pKa, they lose protons and become predominantly ionized. Although the unionized form generally crosses lipid membranes more readily, actual gastrointestinal absorption also depends on surface area, permeability and other factors.
questions.source: General Pharmacology: Drug Absorption - pKa, Ionization and pH Partition
